title: The Science of IOL Power Calculation
summary: Achieving the 'Refractive Bullseye' in cataract surgery requires high-precision biometry and the application of sophisticated mathematical formulas. This guide explores the variables, equations, and clinical considerations essential for selecting the perfect intraocular lens.

sections.title: Red Flags: Risk of Refractive Surprise
content: Post-Refractive Surgery (LASIK/PRK/RK) - standard formulas will fail.
Extreme Axial Lengths: High Myopia (>26.0 mm) or High Hyperopia (<22.0 mm).
History of Silicone Oil tamponade (requires AL correction).
Dense Brunescent Cataracts interfering with optical biometry.

sections.title: Formula Selection Guide
content: Short Eyes (<22mm): Hoffer Q is traditionally favored.
Medium Eyes (22-26mm): Barrett Universal II or SRK/T.
Long Eyes (>26mm): Barrett Universal II or Wang-Koch adjusted SRK/T.
Universal Choice: Barrett Universal II performs well across all ranges.

sections.title: The Calculation Workflow
content: 2. Review K-values for regularity and astigmatism.
3. Select IOL Model (Monofocal, Toric, or Multifocal).
4. Choose formula based on AL and anterior segment data.
5. Optimize A-Constant based on surgeon personal outcomes.

sections.title: Verbatim Clinical Context
sections.content: IOL power calculation is a critical step in cataract surgery that determines the postoperative refractive state. The accuracy of the calculation depends heavily on the precision of biometry (axial length and corneal power) and the mathematical formula used to predict the Effective Lens Position (ELP). Modern biometers use partial coherence interferometry or optical low-coherence reflectometry to provide measurements with micron-level precision, significantly reducing the errors associated with older ultrasound-based immersion or applanation techniques.
